passage: Lalremsiami, you asked how I got through the first weeks, so I'm Reena, and here is what I did. On the second night I sat on the floor and said out loud: these weeks will be heavy. Sleep by eleven, phone in the other room. And one rule: no big decisions on days when I'm crying. No changing courses, no messages to him, no cutting my hair. passage:
I'm Salma, Shankar's classmate, and we share a study table in the library. The week after his girlfriend ended things, I expected him to vanish. Instead, on Monday, he showed me a sheet of paper.
'The next three weeks are going to be bad,' he said, very matter-of-fact. 'So I'm not going to trust my moods. I'm going to trust this.' The sheet said: classes, every one. Lunch at one with you lot. Bed by midnight, phone outside the room. And at the bottom, underlined: Nothing big gets decided on a bad day.
'Like what?' I asked.
'Like dropping the elective. Or shaving my head.' He almost smiled.
Some days he sat through lectures staring at nothing. But he came. Once he told me, 'Today's a bad day, so I'm not deciding about the internship till Friday.' I can't know how heavy it was inside, but by week four he was arguing with the professor again.

qa.q: What was underlined at the bottom of Shankar's sheet?
qa.a: Nothing big gets decided on a bad day.

qa.q: What does Shankar's matter-of-fact 'The next three weeks are going to be bad' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and heavy but clear-headed enough to expect it, so he chose to rely on routine rather than his low moods.

qa.q: What else could Shankar add to the sheet for the hardest evenings?
qa.a: A name to call, like a friend or family member, so the evenings have some company as well as routine.

qa.q: How do those weeks look to Salma at the study table?
qa.a: Salma sees Shankar staring blankly some days but still turning up, and notices the old, argumentative Shankar return by week four.

grounding: Shows a student expecting the first weeks after a breakup to be heavy and planning around it with classes, meals, sleep and no big decisions on bad days.

Day 2, Saturday. Baljeet's relationship of two years ended on Friday night. She sits on her hostel bed with a notebook and writes: 'It will be heavy for a while. That's normal.' Under it: eat three meals, go to every class, lights off by 12, walk with Leela every evening. And a rule: no decisions about the semester exchange until the end of the month.
Day 11, Monday. She wakes at 5 and can't sleep again. She wants to email the exchange office and withdraw, to get away from everything. She opens the notebook, reads the rule, and closes the email. She goes to her 9 a.m. class with swollen eyes.
Day 30, Saturday. The heaviness is lighter, not gone. At a café with Leela, she opens the exchange form again and, calmly, fills it in.

qa.q: Until when did Baljeet decide not to make decisions about the exchange?
qa.a: Until the end of the month.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling on Day 11 when she wanted to withdraw from the exchange?
qa.a: She felt raw and desperate to escape, which is why the pull to withdraw was so strong on a sleepless morning.

qa.q: What else could help Baljeet on mornings like Day 11?
qa.a: Message Leela or another close person early, so a sleepless morning is not faced alone.

qa.q: How might Leela see the evening walks and the café day?
qa.a: Leela likely sees Baljeet slowly steadying, and the calm form-filling at the café shows the plan protected a big decision.

grounding: Shows a student planning the first weeks after a breakup around meals, classes, sleep and walks, and delaying a big decision until the heavy days pass.
